newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE -Italian war crimes case languishes in limbo.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE -Italian war crimes case languishes in limbo.

text.p: A lawyer for Nazi war crimes defendant Erich Priebke says he believes there are those in Italian judicial circles who would like nothing better than for his 83-year-old client to drop dead.
Although speaking tongue-in-cheek, lawyer Giosue Naso says "it's obvious no one wants to touch this case."

Priebke, accused of multiple murder for his involvement in the SS massacre of 335 men and boys in Nazi-occupied Rome in 1944, has been detained in jail in the Italian capital since his extradition from Argentina in November 1995.
Already tried in Italy, but with the controversial verdict thrown out on appeal, Priebke's case is being batted between military and civilian courts: a political hot potato in judicial limbo.
Italy's highest court, the Court of Cassation, meets on Monday to decide which court has jurisdiction to hear the retrial. The judges will have five days to rule.
One has only to look at the outcome of Priebke's first trial to see why a judge may be hesitant to take on the case of the German former SS captain.
RIOT IN ROME
A riot broke out when a military court ruled on August 1 that while Priebke was guilty of multiple murder, extenuating circumstances required that he be set free.
Angry Romans gathered in the corridor outside the courtroom, blocking his way out, and refused to leave. At one point, they tried to storm the courtroom but guards held them back.

The situation was defused only when Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick came to the courthouse and ordered Priebke's re-arrest based on a request by Germany to extradite him for a war crimes trial there.

An appeal threw out the verdict but the political sensitivity, leading both military and civilian courts to beg off hearing the case, brought matters full circle. Once a venue is set, the trial re-starts from scratch.
Antonino Intelisano, the military prosecutor who tried Priebke the first time around, is resigned.
"Obviously the decision to overturn the verdict created delays," he said. "But given the pace of the Italian justice system, this case falls within the average."
DELAYS WORRY ADVERSARIES
Priebke's lawyers say the continued detention of their client is a violation of his rights and are planning to seek recourse in the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.
The Nazi-tracking Simon Wiesenthal Center, which helped locate Priebke at his home of more than 50 years in the Andean ski resort of Bariloche, is also worried by the delays.

"What happens in situations that are drawn out like this is there is a numbing effect, events are replaced by other issues...," said Shimon Samuels, European affairs director for the Los Angeles-based Wiesenthal Center.
"At the end of day there will be total indifference."
Priebke admits he was at the Ardeatine Caves outside the city walls when the 335 victims where shot on March 24, 1944.
He says he checked names off a list as the victims, 75 of the Jews, were led into the caves and admits shooting two.

Priebke says he had to follow orders or be killed himself and adds that the massacre was a "legitimate wartime reprisal" for a partisans' bomb attack the day before in which 33 troops loyal to the Nazis were killed.
LAWYER SEES PLOT THAT BACKFIRED
The Priebke case is not only a victim of the general disarray in the Italian justice system.

Many commentators also regard it as delicate because it touches a raw nerve in Italy itself, a country that has still not fully overcome the divisions sown by its disastrous Fascist alliance with Nazi Germany in World War Two.

Naso said he believes the judicial authorities knew all along that Priebke would be difficult to try, but that "leftist elements" in the Justice Ministry sought his extradition in the spring of 1994 to create an embarrassment for the newly-elected centre-right prime minister, Silvio Berlusconi.
Berlusconi's government was the first to include ministers with links to the Fascist ideology of wartime dictator Benito Mussolini.

"But after eight months, in a typical Italian fashion, one of Berlusconi's partners pulled out of the coalition and his government fell," Naso said. "Then the next government, which was supported by those same leftist elements, found the problem at its feet.
"Judges would like Priebke to resolve the problem through natural causes, by dying," the lawyer added.
